claim: During anaphase B, molecular motors slide interpolar microtubules to elongate the mitotic spindle, contributing to the separation of chromosomes.
source: During anaphase B, molecular motors slide interpolar microtubules to elongate the mitotic spindle, contributing to the separation of chromosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about anaphase B mechanisms.

claim: Sliding of antiparallel microtubules reduces their overlap, which may lead to spindle breakage, unless microtubules grow to compensate sliding.
source: However, sliding of antiparallel microtubules reduces their overlap, which may lead to spindle breakage, unless microtubules grow to compensate sliding.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanical consequences of microtubule sliding.

claim: The coordination of microtubule growth and sliding relies on promoting rescues at the midzone edges.
source: We report that the coordination of microtubule growth and sliding relies on promoting rescues at the midzone edges.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Promoting rescues at the midzone edges makes microtubules stable from pole to midzone, while their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly.
source: This makes microtubules stable from pole to midzone, while their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of rescue localization.

claim: The midzone keeps a constant length throughout anaphase.
source: Consequently, the midzone keeps a constant length throughout anaphase, enabling sustained sliding without the need for a precise regulation of microtubule growth speed.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements.

claim: In S. pombe, which undergoes closed mitosis, microtubule growth speed decreases when the nuclear membrane wraps around the spindle midzone.
source: Additionally, we found that in S. pombe, which undergoes closed mitosis, microtubule growth speed decreases when the nuclear membrane wraps around the spindle midzone.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations.

claim: In certain cells (e.g. PtK2 cells), cortical pulling on astral microtubules is thought to drive spindle elongation during anaphase B.
source: In certain cells (e.g. PtK2 cells) (Aist et al., 1993), cortical pulling on astral microtubules is thought to drive spindle elongation during anaphase B.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In most biological systems studied so far, anaphase B is mainly driven by molecular motors which slide interpolar microtubules at the midzone.
source: However, in most biological systems studied so far (Yu et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2009; Vukušić and Tolić, 2021; Brust-Mascher and Scholey, 2002; Vukušić et al., 2021), this is mainly driven by molecular motors, which slide interpolar microtubules at the midzone, the central spindle region where interpolar microtubules coming from opposite poles are crosslinked antiparallely by members of the PRC1/Ase1 family (Figure 1A; Kapitein et al., 2008; Loiodice et al., 2005; Mollinari et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Interpolar microtubules coming from opposite poles are crosslinked antiparallely by members of the PRC1/Ase1 family at the midzone.
source: However, in most biological systems studied so far (Yu et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2009; Vukušić and Tolić, 2021; Brust-Mascher and Scholey, 2002; Vukušić et al., 2021), this is mainly driven by molecular motors, which slide interpolar microtubules at the midzone, the central spindle region where interpolar microtubules coming from opposite poles are crosslinked antiparallely by members of the PRC1/Ase1 family (Figure 1A; Kapitein et al., 2008; Loiodice et al., 2005; Mollinari et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sliding shortens the overlap between microtubules, such that microtubules must continuously elongate to sustain sliding.
source: Importantly, sliding shortens the overlap between microtubules, such that microtubules must continuously elongate to sustain sliding (Scholey et al., 2016; Vukušić and Tolić, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The midzone length remains roughly constant during anaphase B.
source: Remarkably, the midzone length remains roughly constant during anaphase B (Hu et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2009), indicating that net polymerisation and sliding closely match in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Net polymerisation and sliding closely match in vivo during anaphase B.
source: Remarkably, the midzone length remains roughly constant during anaphase B (Hu et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2009), indicating that net polymerisation and sliding closely match in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that midzone length remains constant.

claim: Purified algae spindles would slide if tubulin was available for microtubules to grow, but would stop sliding in the absence of soluble tubulin.
source: Pioneering studies found that purified algae spindles would slide if tubulin was available for microtubules to grow, but would stop sliding in the absence of soluble tubulin (Masuda et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sliding can be limited by microtubule growth.
source: This showed that sliding can be limited by microtubule growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the algae spindle experiments.

claim: In animal cells, kinesin-4 suppresses the dynamics of interpolar microtubules and could induce growth-limited regime.
source: In animal cells, kinesin-4 suppresses the dynamics of interpolar microtubules and could induce this growth-limited regime (Bieling et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2011; Hannabuss et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and involves speculation about mechanism.

claim: Depletion of kinesin-4, which leads to highly dynamic interpolar microtubules, does not have an impact on anaphase spindle elongation velocity.
source: However, depletion of kinesin-4, which leads to highly dynamic interpolar microtubules (Hu et al., 2011), does not have an impact on anaphase spindle elongation velocity (Vukušić et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeasts lack kinesin-4.
source: Yeasts lack kinesin-4, but their final spindle length is reduced if microtubule dynamics are suppressed by nocodazole treatment or deletion of the microtubule polymerase Stu2 (Rizk et al., 2014), indicating that suppressing microtubule dynamics can arrest sliding.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast.

claim: In yeasts, final spindle length is reduced if microtubule dynamics are suppressed by nocodazole treatment or deletion of the microtubule polymerase Stu2.
source: Yeasts lack kinesin-4, but their final spindle length is reduced if microtubule dynamics are suppressed by nocodazole treatment or deletion of the microtubule polymerase Stu2 (Rizk et al., 2014), indicating that suppressing microtubule dynamics can arrest sliding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Suppressing microtubule dynamics can arrest sliding in yeasts.
source: Yeasts lack kinesin-4, but their final spindle length is reduced if microtubule dynamics are suppressed by nocodazole treatment or deletion of the microtubule polymerase Stu2 (Rizk et al., 2014), indicating that suppressing microtubule dynamics can arrest sliding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that spindle length is reduced when dynamics are suppressed.

claim: Comparable results have been obtained in HeLa cells when depleting TACC3.
source: Comparable results have been obtained in HeLa cells when depleting TACC3 (Lioutas and Vernos, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Growth-limited sliding can happen in a wide range of organisms when microtubule dynamics are suppressed.
source: Therefore, growth-limited sliding can happen in a wide range of organisms when microtubule dynamics are suppressed, but it is not known whether it occurs in unperturbed spindles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: It is not known whether growth-limited sliding occurs in unperturbed spindles.
source: Therefore, growth-limited sliding can happen in a wide range of organisms when microtubule dynamics are suppressed, but it is not known whether it occurs in unperturbed spindles.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A motor could set both the polymerisation and sliding speed of interpolar microtubules.
source: An alternative mechanism for the coordination of sliding and growth has been recently proposed: a motor could set both the polymerisation and sliding speed of interpolar microtubules (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: In fission yeast, Klp9 (kinesin-6) slides microtubules during anaphase.
source: In fission yeast, this would be Klp9 (kinesin-6), which slides microtubules during anaphase (Fu et al., 2009) and promotes microtubule polymerisation in monopolar spindles (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Klp9 promotes microtubule polymerisation in monopolar spindles.
source: In fission yeast, this would be Klp9 (kinesin-6), which slides microtubules during anaphase (Fu et al., 2009) and promotes microtubule polymerisation in monopolar spindles (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Klp9 and the related kinesin-5 regulate microtubule dynamics in vitro.
source: Klp9 and the related kinesin-5 also regulate microtubule dynamics in vitro (Chen and Hancock, 2015; Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Microtubule nucleation could enable sustained sliding by continuously replenishing microtubules in the overlap, similarly to what happens in Xenopus metaphase.
source: Microtubule nucleation could enable sustained sliding by continuously replenishing microtubules in the overlap, similarly to what happens in Xenopus metaphase (Brugués et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Chromosome segregation during anaphase can occur in the absence of nucleation.
source: However, chromosome segregation during anaphase can occur in the absence of nucleation (Julian et al., 1993; Uehara et al., 2009; Uehara and Goshima, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Microtubule rescue is required during anaphase in Xenopus and S. pombe.
source: On the other hand, microtubule rescue is required during anaphase in Xenopus and S. pombe, and in the absence of the rescue promoting factor CLASP, spindle microtubules fully depolymerise at anaphase onset (Hannak and Heald, 2006; Bratman and Chang, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the absence of the rescue promoting factor CLASP, spindle microtubules fully depolymerise at anaphase onset.
source: On the other hand, microtubule rescue is required during anaphase in Xenopus and S. pombe, and in the absence of the rescue promoting factor CLASP, spindle microtubules fully depolymerise at anaphase onset (Hannak and Heald, 2006; Bratman and Chang, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeasts undergo closed mitosis where their nuclear membrane does not disassemble during mitosis.
source: Finally, yeasts undergo closed mitosis: their nuclear membrane does not disassemble during mitosis, and in anaphase B it constricts to form a dumbbell shape with a thin nuclear bridge around the spindle (Dey et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In anaphase B of yeasts, the nuclear membrane constricts to form a dumbbell shape with a thin nuclear bridge around the spindle.
source: Finally, yeasts undergo closed mitosis: their nuclear membrane does not disassemble during mitosis, and in anaphase B it constricts to form a dumbbell shape with a thin nuclear bridge around the spindle (Dey et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At the end of anaphase in yeasts, the nuclear membrane disassembles locally at the bridge, exposing the spindle to cytoplasmic factors that trigger spindle disassembly.
source: At the end of anaphase, the nuclear membrane disassembles locally at the bridge, exposing the spindle to cytoplasmic factors that trigger spindle disassembly (Lucena et al., 2015; Dey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Les1, an inner nuclear membrane protein, forms two stalks at the sides of the bridge that restrict nuclear membrane disassembly to the spindle center and seal the edges of the severed bridge preventing leakage of nuclear content.
source: Les1, an inner nuclear membrane protein, forms two stalks at the sides of the bridge that restrict nuclear membrane disassembly to the spindle center and seal the edges of the severed bridge preventing leakage of nuclear content (Dey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ase1 midzone crosslinkers are required for the sorting of nuclear pore complexes in the nuclear membrane bridge.
source: For example, Ase1 midzone crosslinkers are required for the sorting of nuclear pore complexes in the nuclear membrane bridge (Expósito-Serrano et al., 2020), and for the nuclear bridge to act as a diffusion barrier between daughter nuclei (Boettcher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ase1 midzone crosslinkers are required for the nuclear bridge to act as a diffusion barrier between daughter nuclei.
source: For example, Ase1 midzone crosslinkers are required for the sorting of nuclear pore complexes in the nuclear membrane bridge (Expósito-Serrano et al., 2020), and for the nuclear bridge to act as a diffusion barrier between daughter nuclei (Boettcher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FRAP has been used to establish that microtubule turnover during anaphase B is lower than during metaphase in Drosophila and yeast.
source: FRAP has been used to infer certain aspects in cells expressing fluorescent tubulin, establishing that microtubule turnover during anaphase B is lower than during metaphase in Drosophila and yeast (Brust-Mascher et al., 2004; Brust-Mascher et al., 2015; Mallavarapu et al., 1999; Higuchi and Uhlmann, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In yeast no microtubule nucleation occurs during anaphase B.
source: These experiments also showed that in yeast no microtubule nucleation occurs during anaphase B, and that interpolar microtubules are maintained through rescues (Khodjakov et al., 2004).

claim: Interpolar microtubules are maintained through rescues during anaphase B in yeast.
source: These experiments also showed that in yeast no microtubule nucleation occurs during anaphase B, and that interpolar microtubules are maintained through rescues (Khodjakov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fluorescently labelled tubulin was used in yeast to image microtubule dynamics during anaphase B, but growth events were only resolvable at very late anaphase, when the spindle is composed of approximately four microtubules.
source: Fluorescently labelled tubulin was used in yeast to image microtubule dynamics during anaphase B, but growth events were only resolvable at very late anaphase, when the spindle is composed of approximately four microtubules (Sagolla et al., 2003).

claim: A recent report used RPE-1 cells expressing labelled EB1 and found that microtubule growth speed decreases with anaphase B progression.

claim: Live-imaging of S. pombe cells expressing Alp7-3xGFP allows visualization of microtubule dynamics during anaphase B.
source: Live-imaging of S. pombe cells expressing Alp7-3xGFP allows to visualise microtubule dynamics during anaphase B
evidence: This is a methodological finding based on the experimental approach described.

claim: Alp7 is the S. pombe orthologue of mammalian Transforming Acidic Coiled-Coil (TACC).
source: Alp7 is the S. pombe orthologue of mammalian Transforming Acidic Coiled-Coil (TACC) (Sato et al., 2004), and forms a complex with the XMAP215 orthologue Alp14, a microtubule polymerase (Al-Bassam et al., 2012).

claim: Alp7 forms a complex with the XMAP215 orthologue Alp14, a microtubule polymerase.
source: Alp7 is the S. pombe orthologue of mammalian Transforming Acidic Coiled-Coil (TACC) (Sato et al., 2004), and forms a complex with the XMAP215 orthologue Alp14, a microtubule polymerase (Al-Bassam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Alp7/Alp14 complex localises to Spindle Pole Bodies (SPBs) and microtubule plus ends.
source: The Alp7/Alp14 complex localises to Spindle Pole Bodies (SPBs) and microtubule plus ends (Sato et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In S. pombe all the minus ends of interpolar microtubules are located at the SPBs.
source: Given that in S. pombe all the minus ends of interpolar microtubules are located at the SPBs (Ward et al., 2014; Ding et al., 1993), microtubule length can be measured as the distance between the plus end and the pole located opposite to the direction of growth (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The duration of microtubule growth events did not change during anaphase B and was on average 52 ± 23 s.
source: We found that the duration of microtubule growth events did not change during anaphase B and was on average 52 ± 23 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements.

claim: Microtubule shrinking speed did not change during anaphase and was on average 3.55 ± 1.62 μm/min.
source: Microtubule shrinking speed did not change during anaphase either (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and was on average 3.55 ± 1.62 μm/min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements.

claim: Microtubule growth velocity decreased during anaphase B.
source: On the other hand, microtubule growth velocity decreased during anaphase B (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Two populations of microtubules (fast and slow growing) are characteristic of early and late anaphase.
source: Furthermore, this decrease was not gradual, and we observed two populations of microtubules (fast and slow growing) characteristic of early and late anaphase.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: In some cells, all microtubules seemed to switch to the slow growing phase simultaneously.
source: In some cells, all microtubules seemed to switch to the slow growing phase simultaneously (Figure 1C), while in others fast and slow growing microtubules co-existed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The microtubule growth velocities of the two states were 1.60 μm/min and 0.67 μm/min.
source: The microtubule growth velocities of these two states, extracted from the fit, were 1.60 μm/min and 0.67 μm/min.
evidence: This is a finding based on data analysis.

claim: Most microtubule rescues occurred near the spindle midzone.
source: In our dataset, most microtubule rescues occurred near the spindle midzone.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Cls1 (CLASP), a MAP required for microtubule rescue, is recruited to the midzone by Ase1 crosslinkers.
source: This is likely due to the fact that Cls1 (CLASP), a MAP required for microtubule rescue, is recruited to the midzone by Ase1 crosslinkers (Bratman and Chang, 2007).

claim: 93% of the rescues happened at positive positions relative to the spindle center.
source: This revealed that rescues did not occur uniformly along the midzone, since 93% of the rescues happened at positive positions (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure.

claim: The positions where most rescues happened coincided with the edge of the midzone, measured from Cls1-3xGFP signal.
source: Moreover, the positions where most rescues happened coincided with the edge of the midzone, measured from Cls1-3xGFP signal in another strain (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: The duration of microtubule growth events was the same in cells expressing GFP-Mal3 and Alp7-3xGFP.
source: We found that the duration of microtubule growth events was the same in cells expressing GFP-Mal3 and Alp7-3xGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, C), while in cells expressing GFP-Mal3, microtubule growth speed was slightly lower and rescues occurred slightly closer to the center than in cells expressing Alp7-3xGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: In cells expressing GFP-Mal3, microtubule growth speed was slightly lower and rescues occurred slightly closer to the center than in cells expressing Alp7-3xGFP.
source: We found that the duration of microtubule growth events was the same in cells expressing GFP-Mal3 and Alp7-3xGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, C), while in cells expressing GFP-Mal3, microtubule growth speed was slightly lower and rescues occurred slightly closer to the center than in cells expressing Alp7-3xGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: Alp7-3xGFP is a reliable marker for microtubule dynamics.
source: These differences are minor, so we concluded that Alp7-3xGFP is a reliable marker for microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of GFP-Mal3 and Alp7-3xGFP data.

claim: GFP-Mal3 signal was lost from the spindle at late anaphase B.
source: Notably, GFP-Mal3 signal was lost from the spindle at late anaphase B (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), making it impossible to track plus ends.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Alp7-3xGFP remains at microtubule plus ends at late anaphase, making it a better marker for microtubule dynamics during anaphase.
source: In contrast, Alp7-3xGFP remains at microtubule plus ends at late anaphase, making it a better marker for microtubule dynamics during anaphase.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Both microtubule growth event duration and speed were lower during anaphase B compared to interphase.
source: We found that both microtubule growth event duration and speed were lower during anaphase B (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: Bim1 (Orthologue of Mal3/EB1 in S. cerevisiae) is phosphorylated at late anaphase by Aurora B, which reduces its affinity for microtubules.
source: Bim1 (Orthologue of Mal3/EB1 in S. cerevisiae) is phosphorylated at late anaphase by Aurora B, which reduces its affinity for microtubules (Zimniak et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Bim1 mutants that cannot be phosphorylated delay spindle disassembly.
source: In addition, Bim1 mutants that cannot be phosphorylated delay spindle disassembly (Zimniak et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In S. pombe, Mal3 is phosphorylated in a cell-cycle-dependent manner.
source: In S. pombe, Mal3 is also phosphorylated in a cell-cycle-dependent manner (Iimori et al., 2012), and mutant Mal3 constructs mimicking this phosphorylation have lower microtubule growth promoting activity in vitro than wild-type Mal3 (Iimori et al., 2012).

claim: Mutant Mal3 constructs mimicking phosphorylation have lower microtubule growth promoting activity in vitro than wild-type Mal3.
source: In S. pombe, Mal3 is also phosphorylated in a cell-cycle-dependent manner (Iimori et al., 2012), and mutant Mal3 constructs mimicking this phosphorylation have lower microtubule growth promoting activity in vitro than wild-type Mal3 (Iimori et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: mal3Δ cells exhibited lower microtubule growth speed throughout anaphase B.
source: As expected, considering that Mal3 promotes microtubule growth (Busch and Brunner, 2004), mal3Δ cells exhibited lower microtubule growth speed throughout anaphase B (Figure 2B and G).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: A reduction of microtubule growth could still be observed with anaphase progression in mal3Δ cells.
source: However, a reduction of microtubule growth could still be observed with anaphase progression, and normalised microtubule growth velocities were distributed similarly in wild-type and mal3Δ cells (Figure 2H), suggesting that Mal3 is not required for the reduction of microtubule growth speed in anaphase B.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure.

claim: Mal3 is not required for the reduction of microtubule growth speed in anaphase B.
source: However, a reduction of microtubule growth could still be observed with anaphase progression, and normalised microtubule growth velocities were distributed similarly in wild-type and mal3Δ cells (Figure 2H), suggesting that Mal3 is not required for the reduction of microtubule growth speed in anaphase B.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: S. cerevisiae Kip3 (kinesin-8) is a plus end directed motor that localises to the anaphase B spindle and suppresses microtubule dynamics in a length-dependent manner.
source: S. cerevisiae Kip3 (kinesin-8) is a plus end directed motor that localises to the anaphase B spindle and suppresses microtubule dynamics in a length-dependent manner (Gardner et al., 2011; Rizk et al., 2014).

claim: In S. pombe interphase, the kinesin-8 heterodimer Klp5/Klp6 accumulates at plus ends in a length-dependent manner, promoting catastrophe.
source: In S. pombe interphase, the kinesin-8 heterodimer Klp5/Klp6 accumulates at plus ends in a length-dependent manner, promoting catastrophe (Tischer et al., 2009), so Klp5/Klp6 could trigger the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth during anaphase.

claim: klp5Δklp6Δ cells exhibited slightly longer microtubule growth events.
source: As expected, klp5Δklp6Δ cells exhibited slightly longer microtubule growth events (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: The decrease in microtubule growth speed is independent of Klp5/Klp6.
source: However, the distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue was not very different from wild-type cells (Figure 2C, I), indicating that the decrease in microtubule growth speed is independent of Klp5/Klp6.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Cls1 is required for microtubule rescues to occur during anaphase in S. pombe.
source: Cls1 is required for microtubule rescues to occur during anaphase in S. pombe (Bratman and Chang, 2007), and it decreases microtubule growth speed in a dose-dependent manner (Bratman and Chang, 2007; Al-Bassam et al., 2010).

claim: Cls1 decreases microtubule growth speed in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Cls1 is required for microtubule rescues to occur during anaphase in S. pombe (Bratman and Chang, 2007), and it decreases microtubule growth speed in a dose-dependent manner (Bratman and Chang, 2007; Al-Bassam et al., 2010).

claim: Cls1 levels on the spindle remained constant throughout anaphase B.
source: We measured Cls1 levels on the spindle and found that they remained constant throughout anaphase B (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure.

claim: The density of Cls1 on microtubules increases during anaphase B as the number of microtubules in the spindle decreases.
source: However, as the number of microtubules in the spindle decreases with anaphase B progression (Ward et al., 2014; Ding et al., 1993), the density of Cls1 on microtubules increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and this might reduce growth speed.

source: Additionally, as in mal3Δ cells, the normalised growth speeds were distributed similarly to wild-type in both cls1off and cls1OE cells (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).

claim: The transition of microtubule growth speed occurred across a wide range of Cls1 levels, arguing against a role of Cls1 in this transition.

claim: Klp9 (kinesin-6) is the main driver of microtubule sliding during anaphase B.

claim: Klp9 promotes microtubule growth in vitro and is required for the elongation of bundles of parallel microtubules present in monopolar spindles that undergo metaphase to anaphase transition.
source: Klp9 promotes microtubule growth in vitro and is required for the elongation of bundles of parallel microtubules present in monopolar spindles that undergo metaphase to anaphase transition (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

source: Notably, the bundle elongation velocity matches the microtubule sliding speed in bipolar spindles, suggesting that Klp9 might set both microtubule growth and sliding speed in bipolar spindles.

claim: klp9 deletion reduced spindle elongation velocity.
source: As expected (Fu et al., 2009), klp9 deletion reduced spindle elongation velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Recruitment of Klp9 to the spindle midzone relies on the dephosphorylation of its Cdk1 phosphosites at anaphase onset.
source: Recruitment of Klp9 to the spindle midzone relies on the dephosphorylation of its Cdk1 phosphosites at anaphase onset (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This dephosphorylation occurs through two independent pathways involving the phosphatase Clp1 (orthologue of Cdc14) and the XMAP215 microtubule polymerase Dis1.
source: This dephosphorylation occurs through two independent pathways involving the phosphatase Clp1 (orthologue of Cdc14) (Fu et al., 2009; Wolfe and Gould, 2004; Esteban et al., 2004), and the XMAP215 microtubule polymerase Dis1 (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: clp1Δ and dis1Δ cells had an identical phenotype to klp9Δ cells: their spindle elongation velocity was slower during anaphase, but distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue was similar to wild-type.
source: clp1Δ and dis1Δ cells had an identical phenotype to klp9Δ cells: their spindle elongation velocity was slower during anaphase, but distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue was similar to wild-type (Figure 2F and L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), indicating that neither the dephosphorylation of Cdk1 phosphosites mediated by Clp1 nor the activity of Dis1 are required for the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth velocity to occur during anaphase B.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: Neither the dephosphorylation of Cdk1 phosphosites mediated by Clp1 nor the activity of Dis1 are required for the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth velocity to occur during anaphase B.
source: clp1Δ and dis1Δ cells had an identical phenotype to klp9Δ cells: their spindle elongation velocity was slower during anaphase, but distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue was similar to wild-type (Figure 2F and L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), indicating that neither the dephosphorylation of Cdk1 phosphosites mediated by Clp1 nor the activity of Dis1 are required for the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth velocity to occur during anaphase B.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The positions of microtubule rescues were clustered as in wild-type across all conditions.
source: Finally, the positions of microtubule rescues were clustered as in wild-type across all conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure.

claim: In mal3Δ and klp5Δklp6Δ cells, the average position of rescues with respect to the spindle center was markedly higher than in wild-type.
source: In mal3Δ and klp5Δklp6Δ cells, the average position of rescues with respect to the spindle center was markedly higher than in wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: The transition from fast to slow microtubule growth during anaphase occurs in the absence of multiple MAPs associated with the mitotic spindle known to affect microtubule dynamics in a different context or organism.
source: In summary, our experiments show that the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth during anaphase occurs in the absence of multiple MAPs associated with the mitotic spindle known to affect microtubule dynamics in a different context or organism.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of the distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue is maintained even in cells where spindle elongation is slower.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of the distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue is maintained even in cells where spindle elongation is slower, suggesting that microtubule growth velocity during anaphase B could be affected by spatial cues associated with the spindle.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Microtubule growth velocity during anaphase B could be affected by spatial cues associated with the spindle.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of the distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue is maintained even in cells where spindle elongation is slower, suggesting that microtubule growth velocity during anaphase B could be affected by spatial cues associated with the spindle.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The slow growing microtubules were the ones inside the nuclear membrane bridge.
source: Imaging strains expressing the nuclear membrane marker Cut11-mCherry (Figure 3A), we noticed that the slow growing microtubules were the ones inside the nuclear membrane bridge (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Wild-type, klp9OE and cdc25-22 nuclei underwent dumbbell transition at different spindle lengths.
source: Wild-type, klp9OEand cdc25-22 nuclei underwent dumbbell transition at different spindle lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), and their distribution of microtubule growth speed as a function of time, spindle length or distance from the plus end to the closest pole at rescue were different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures.

claim: Microtubule growth velocity in each category (before, inside, outside) was not different for wt, klp9OE and cdc25-22 cells.
source: However, regression analysis showed that if we categorised microtubule growth events depending on whether they occurred 'before' the dumbbell transition, and 'inside' or 'outside' the nuclear membrane bridge (cartoons in Figure 3D), microtubule growth velocity in each category was not different for wt, klp9OE and cdc25-22 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of data shown in a figure.

claim: A linear model taking into account only the categorisation (before, inside, outside) explained 48% of the variability in microtubule growth speed.
source: In fact, a linear model taking into account only this categorisation, explained 48% of the variability (see Statistical Analysis).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of data.

claim: The 13% decrease in growth speed observed between 'before' and 'outside' events was minor compared to the 60% reduction when comparing 'before' and 'inside'.
source: The 13% decrease in growth speed observed between 'before' and 'outside' events was minor compared to the 60% reduction when comparing 'before' and 'inside' (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding based on data analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Microtubules grow slower when they enter the nuclear membrane bridge formed by the dumbbell transition.
source: From this direct imaging we conclude that microtubules grow slower when they enter the nuclear membrane bridge formed by the dumbbell transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Treating cells with 10 µM of cerulenin prevented dumbbell transition and abolished the decrease in microtubule growth speed.
source: Treating cells with 10 µM of cerulenin prevented dumbbell transition, and abolished the decrease in microtubule growth speed (Figure 4C and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: In wild-type and 'ark1-as3 normal' cells, microtubules grew slower inside the nuclear membrane bridge.
source: In wild-type and 'ark1-as3 normal' cells, microtubules grew slower inside the nuclear membrane bridge (Figure 4I, Appendix 1—table 2), but in 'ark1-as3 abnormal' cells microtubule growth velocity was not significantly different (p-value 0.38, see Statistical Analysis) outside or inside the nuclear membrane tubes formed at the spindle poles (Figure 4F, I Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures and tables.

claim: In 'ark1-as3 abnormal' cells microtubule growth velocity was not significantly different outside or inside the nuclear membrane tubes formed at the spindle poles.
source: In wild-type and 'ark1-as3 normal' cells, microtubules grew slower inside the nuclear membrane bridge (Figure 4I, Appendix 1—table 2), but in 'ark1-as3 abnormal' cells microtubule growth velocity was not significantly different (p-value 0.38, see Statistical Analysis) outside or inside the nuclear membrane tubes formed at the spindle poles (Figure 4F, I Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in figures.

claim: The transition from fast to slow microtubule growth can happen upon Aurora B inactivation, but not if chromosome segregation fails and the dumbbell transition is prevented.
source: This data shows that the transition from fast to slow microtubule growth can happen upon Aurora B inactivation, but not if chromosome segregation fails and the dumbbell transition is prevented.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Microtubule growth speed can remain unchanged for a period of time as long as wild-type anaphase B if the dumbbell transition is prevented.
source: In summary, our data shows that microtubule growth speed can remain unchanged for a period of time as long as wild-type anaphase B if the dumbbell transition is prevented (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The decrease in microtubule growth speed observed in wild-type cells is not regulated by a 'timer' mechanism, but instead occurs when the nuclear membrane bridge encloses the midzone.
source: This suggests that the decrease in microtubule growth speed observed in wild-type cells is not regulated by a 'timer' mechanism, but instead occurs when the nuclear membrane bridge encloses the midzone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: In both les1Δ and nem1Δ cells microtubule growth speed inside the nuclear bridge was faster than in wild-type cells, while the microtubule growth speed outside the nuclear bridge was unaffected.
source: We found that in both les1Δ and nem1Δ cells microtubule growth speed inside the nuclear bridge was faster than in wild-type cells, while the microtubule growth speed outside the nuclear bridge was unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–F, Appendix 1—table 5, Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in figures and tables.

claim: The formation of Les1 stalks is required for the normal decrease of microtubule growth speed when microtubule plus ends enter the nuclear membrane bridge.
source: This data suggests that the formation of Les1 stalks (which potentially promote close interaction of spindle microtubules with the nuclear envelope) is required for the normal decrease of microtubule growth speed when microtubule plus ends enter the nuclear membrane bridge.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Preventing the decrease in microtubule growth speed by cerulenin treatment or Aurora B inhibition did not compromise spindle stability nor overall microtubule organisation.
source: Preventing the decrease in microtubule growth speed by cerulenin treatment or Aurora B inhibition did not compromise spindle stability nor overall microtubule organisation.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Since rescues occur most often at midzone edges, microtubules are stable from pole to midzone, and only their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly phases.
source: In fact, since rescues occur most often at midzone edges (Figure 1G), microtubules are stable from pole to midzone, and only their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly phases (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: In cells where ase1 was deleted the characteristic distribution of rescues was lost and spindles collapsed due to loss of microtubule overlaps before reaching the typical final length.
source: As expected (Loiodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005; Bratman and Chang, 2007), in cells where ase1 was deleted the characteristic distribution of rescues was lost (Figure 5B and E) and spindles collapsed due to loss of microtubule overlaps before reaching the typical final length (Figure 5B–D Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures, supported by citations.

claim: The microtubule growth speed was higher throughout anaphase in ase1Δ when compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the microtubule growth speed was higher throughout anaphase in ase1Δ when compared to wild-type, but also that the decrease in microtubule growth between 'before' and 'inside' categories was ∼25%, half of the ∼50% decrease observed in wild-type cells (Figure 5F, Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure and table.

claim: The decrease in microtubule growth between 'before' and 'inside' categories was ∼25% in ase1Δ cells, half of the ∼50% decrease observed in wild-type cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the microtubule growth speed was higher throughout anaphase in ase1Δ when compared to wild-type, but also that the decrease in microtubule growth between 'before' and 'inside' categories was ∼25%, half of the ∼50% decrease observed in wild-type cells (Figure 5F, Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental measurements shown in a figure and table.

claim: Ase1 is required for rescue organisation and for microtubule growth speed to decrease normally during anaphase B.
source: In summary, Ase1 is required for rescue organisation and for microtubule growth speed to decrease normally during anaphase B.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Anaphase B spindles were robust against perturbations on microtubule growth but sensitive to rescue distribution.
source: Our observations showed that anaphase B spindles were robust against perturbations on microtubule growth (Figure 4), but sensitive to rescue distribution (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Promoting rescues at the midzone edges is sufficient to coordinate microtubule sliding and growth.
source: Therefore, we asked whether restricting rescues to the midzone edges is sufficient to coordinate microtubule sliding and growth.
evidence: This is a question addressed by the modeling study.

claim: The spindle is initially composed of nine antiparallel microtubules in the model.
source: Simulations are initialised with a 4 μm long spindle, with 9 microtubules of 3 μm of length arranged in a square lattice as shown in Figure 6A.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: For microtubule growth speed characteristic of early anaphase (1.6 μm/min), the spindle stability was not affected by the distribution of rescue rate within the midzone.
source: For microtubule growth speed characteristic of early anaphase (1.6 μm/min), the spindle stability was not affected by the distribution of rescue rate within the midzone (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations shown in a figure.

claim: Promoting rescues at midzone edges is sufficient to maintain the microtubule overlap and sustain sliding across a wide range of microtubule growth speeds.
source: In summary, this simple model shows that promoting rescues at midzone edges is sufficient to maintain the microtubule overlap and sustain sliding across a wide range of microtubule growth speeds (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations shown in a figure.

claim: Accumulating the rescue activity at the midzone edges might represent an optimal localisation of this activity, in the context of anaphase B.
source: Within our limited exploration, it suggests that accumulating the rescue activity at the midzone edges might represent an optimal localisation of this activity, in the context of anaphase B.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results.

claim: Assuming that a fixed amount of rescue factor distributes along overlaps makes rescue rate proportional to the number of neighbours of a microtubule.
source: Additionally, assuming that a fixed amount of rescue factor distributes along overlaps makes rescue rate proportional to the number of neighbours of a microtubule (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a consequence of the model assumptions shown in a figure.

claim: When a microtubule fully depolymerises, its neighbours oriented in the opposite direction lose one neighbour, while the microtubules in the same orientation as the lost one keep the same number of neighbours, promoting even loss of microtubules from both poles.
source: Therefore, when a microtubule fully depolymerises, its neighbours oriented in the opposite direction lose one neighbour, while the microtubules in the same orientation as the lost one keep the same number of neighbours. This simple effect promotes even loss of microtubules from both poles (Figure 7D), which is necessary to prevent spindle collapse during anaphase B in S. pombe.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model mechanism shown in a figure.

claim: In 500 simulations with parameters as in Figure 6B and C, where spindles start anaphase with nine microtubules, and have on average five microtubules after 15 min, no spindle collapse was observed.
source: In 500 simulations with parameters as in Figure 6B and C, where spindles start anaphase with nine microtubules, and have on average five microtubules after 15 min (the typical duration of anaphase B) we observed no spindle collapse (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations shown in a figure.

claim: The loss of rescue organisation observed in ase1Δ cells could be partly responsible for spindle collapse.
source: Finally, we tested whether the loss of rescue organisation observed in ase1Δ cells (Figure 5E) could be partly responsible for spindle collapse (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by modeling.

claim: Wrapping of the nuclear membrane around the spindle midzone reduces microtubule growth speed.
source: We have measured microtubule dynamics during anaphase B in S. pombe to examine how microtubule polymerisation and sliding are coordinated. We found that: (1) Wrapping of the nuclear membrane around the spindle midzone reduces microtubule growth speed.
evidence: This is a primary finding summarized in the discussion.

claim: Rescues occur preferentially at midzone edges.
source: We have measured microtubule dynamics during anaphase B in S. pombe to examine how microtubule polymerisation and sliding are coordinated. We found that: (1) Wrapping of the nuclear membrane around the spindle midzone reduces microtubule growth speed. (2) Rescues occur preferentially at midzone edges.
evidence: This is a primary finding summarized in the discussion.

claim: Organising rescues at midzone edges is sufficient to coordinate microtubule growth and sliding across the wide range of microtubule growth speeds observed experimentally.
source: We then developed a model showing that organising rescues in this manner is sufficient to coordinate microtubule growth and sliding across the wide range of microtubule growth speeds observed experimentally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling study.

claim: In animal cells, microtubule dynamics are increasingly suppressed during anaphase B by kinesin-4.
source: In animal cells, microtubule dynamics are increasingly suppressed during anaphase B by kinesin-4 (Hu et al., 2011; Nunes Bastos et al., 2013; Asthana et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In S. pombe, which lacks kinesin-4, microtubule growth speed also decreases during anaphase B.
source: We have found that in S. pombe, which lacks kinesin-4, microtubule growth speed also decreases during anaphase B (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Microtubules do not switch to the slow growing state if bridge formation is prevented by cerulenin treatment or Aurora B inhibition.
source: Furthermore, microtubules do not switch to the slow growing state if bridge formation is prevented by cerulenin treatment or Aurora B inhibition (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Microtubule growth speed is mainly governed by spatial cues, rather than a 'timer'.
source: Our data suggests that microtubule growth speed is mainly governed by spatial cues, rather than a 'timer' (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which is reminiscent of recent studies showing that late mitotic events respond to spindle length and not time (Afonso et al., 2014; Afonso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in figures, supported by citations.

claim: ase1 and les1 deletions reduce the decrease in growth speed associated with internalisation of microtubules in the nuclear membrane bridge while also perturbing the sorting of nuclear pore complexes to the center of the nuclear membrane bridge.
source: ase1 and les1 deletions reduce the decrease in growth speed associated with internalisation of microtubules in the nuclear membrane bridge (Figure 5F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) while also perturbing the sorting of nuclear pore complexes to the center of the nuclear membrane bridge (Expósito-Serrano et al., 2020; Dey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures, combined with cited knowledge.

claim: Completely preventing the decrease in microtubule growth speed, delaying it, or reducing its extent did not compromise spindle stability nor overall microtubule organisation.
source: Nevertheless, at least in fission yeast, we could not here assign a biological function to this decrease in microtubule growth speed, as completely preventing it (Figure 4), delaying it (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) or reducing its extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) did not compromise spindle stability nor overall microtubule organisation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Klp9 has no noticeable effect on microtubule growth speed, despite its growth promoting activity in monopolar spindles.
source: Klp9 has no noticeable effect on microtubule growth speed, despite its growth promoting activity in monopolar spindles (Krüger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations, combined with cited knowledge.

claim: Although microtubule growth speed decreases by ∼60%, spindle elongation speed remains constant throughout anaphase B.
source: We have not seen growth-limited sliding in unperturbed spindles either: although microtubule growth speed decreases by ∼60% (Figure 1F), spindle elongation speed remains constant throughout anaphase B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: In S. cerevisiae and Drosophila, deletion or depletion of Kinesin-8, which decreases catastrophe rate, increases sliding speed and final spindle length.
source: In S. cerevisiae and Drosophila, deletion or depletion of Kinesin-8, which decreases catastrophe rate (Wang et al., 2010; Rizk et al., 2014), increases sliding speed and final spindle length (Wang et al., 2010; Rizk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, deletion of kinesin-8 kip3 also delays spindle disassembly.
source: On the other hand, in S. cerevisiae, deletion of kinesin-8 kip3 also delays spindle disassembly (Woodruff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Other mutations that delay spindle disassembly (like cdh1Δ, which prevents the degradation of midzone crosslinkers) produce hyperelongated spindles, similarly to kip3 deletion.
source: Other mutations that delay spindle disassembly (like cdh1Δ, which prevents the degradation of midzone crosslinkers) produce hyperelongated spindles, similarly to kip3 deletion (Woodruff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In both kip3Δ and cdh1Δ, spindle elongation only stops when spindles are cut by the cytokinetic ring.
source: In both kip3Δ and cdh1Δ, spindle elongation only stops when spindles are cut by the cytokinetic ring (Woodruff et al., 2010), suggesting that no mechanism exists to stop sliding during anaphase B other than the disassembly of the midzone, and the same has been observed in S. pombe (Lucena et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No mechanism exists to stop sliding during anaphase B other than the disassembly of the midzone in S. cerevisiae and S. pombe.
source: In both kip3Δ and cdh1Δ, spindle elongation only stops when spindles are cut by the cytokinetic ring (Woodruff et al., 2010), suggesting that no mechanism exists to stop sliding during anaphase B other than the disassembly of the midzone, and the same has been observed in S. pombe (Lucena et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited work.

claim: Growth-limited sliding does not seem to occur in HeLa cells, as depletion of kinesin-4 does not affect spindle elongation velocity.
source: Growth-limited sliding does not seem to occur in HeLa cells either, as depletion of kinesin-4 does not affect spindle elongation velocity (Vukušić et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited work.

claim: Growth-limited sliding is widely conserved, and may contribute to spindle stability in S. pombe when microtubule dynamics are perturbed, such as during starvation.
source: Nevertheless, growth-limited sliding is widely conserved, and may contribute to spindle stability in S. pombe when microtubule dynamics are perturbed, such as during starvation (Tanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The microtubule rescue factor Cls1 (CLASP) is recruited to the midzone by the crosslinker Ase1 (PRC1) in several species.
source: The microtubule rescue factor Cls1 (CLASP) is recruited to the midzone by the crosslinker Ase1 (PRC1) in several species (Liu et al., 2009; Bratman and Chang, 2007; Kitazawa et al., 2014), and it had been previously proposed that this would restrict rescues to the midzone (Bratman and Chang, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spindle microtubules remain stable from the pole to the midzone edge, and only their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly.
source: Thus, spindle microtubules remain stable from the pole to the midzone edge, and only their distal parts including the plus ends alternate between assembly and disassembly (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: S. pombe cells adopted the mechanism of promoting microtubule rescue at midzone edges to ensure spindle integrity, rather than a precise regulation of microtubule growth.
source: Our study suggests that S. pombe cells adopted this mechanism to ensure spindle integrity, rather than a precise regulation of microtubule growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Deletion of Ase1 and inactivation of Cls1 lead to spindle collapse, while perturbing the normal microtubule growth speed evolution during anaphase B has no effect on spindle stability or organisation.
source: This is supported by the fact that deletion of Ase1 (Loiodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005) and inactivation of Cls1 (Bratman and Chang, 2007) lead to spindle collapse, while perturbing the normal microtubule growth speed evolution during anaphase B has no effect on spindle stability or organisation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in a figure, combined with cited knowledge.

claim: In HeLa cells, depletion of kinesin-4 leads to highly dynamic interpolar microtubules, but spindles still elongate with normal speed during anaphase B.
source: In animal cells, the situation is likely more complex: in HeLa cells, depletion of kinesin-4 leads to highly dynamic interpolar microtubules (Hu et al., 2011), but spindles still elongate with normal speed during anaphase B (Vukušić et al., 2021), indicating that a precise regulation of microtubule growth is not required.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Depletion of PRC1/Ase1 does not lead to spindle collapse during anaphase B in HeLa cells.
source: However, depletion of PRC1/Ase1 does not lead to spindle collapse during anaphase B either (Vukušić et al., 2021; Pamula et al., 2019), suggesting that if microtubule rescue organisation is required for spindle stability, it may rely on a mechanism other than recruitment of CLASP by PRC1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The distances between adjacent microtubules in the midzone are comparable to the radius of curling protofilaments.
source: Indeed, the distances between adjacent microtubules in the midzone are comparable to the radius of curling protofilaments (McIntosh et al., 2008; Ward et al., 2014), such that steric collisions alone could promote protofilament straightening, enhancing rescue similarly to what has been proposed for kinetochore protein Dam1 (Franck et al., 2007; McIntosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Steric collisions alone could promote protofilament straightening, enhancing rescue similarly to what has been proposed for kinetochore protein Dam1.
source: Indeed, the distances between adjacent microtubules in the midzone are comparable to the radius of curling protofilaments (McIntosh et al., 2008; Ward et al., 2014), such that steric collisions alone could promote protofilament straightening, enhancing rescue similarly to what has been proposed for kinetochore protein Dam1 (Franck et al., 2007; McIntosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A mechanism to coordinate microtubule sliding and growth relying on rescue localisation is robust against perturbations in polymerisation speed and allows for an array of antiparallel microtubules with a given overlap to continuously elongate.
source: In summary, a mechanism to coordinate microtubule sliding and growth relying on rescue localisation is robust against perturbations in polymerisation speed and allows for an array of antiparallel microtubules with a given overlap to continuously elongate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling study.
